title: Loops — while, do-while, for
summary: Loops repeat code. `while` repeats as long as a condition holds. `do-while` runs the body at least once. `for` is built for counting. `break` leaves a loop and `continue` skips to the next round.
markdown:
## Three loops, one idea

All three repeat a block while a condition is true. They differ in **when** the condition is tested and **where** the counting lives.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph W["while: test first"]
        w1{"condition?"} -- true --> w2["body"] --> w1
        w1 -- false --> w3["done"]
    end
    subgraph D["do-while: test last"]
        d1["body"] --> d2{"condition?"}
        d2 -- true --> d1
        d2 -- false --> d3["done"]
    end
    subgraph F["for: counting built in"]
        f0["start"] --> f1{"condition?"} -- true --> f2["body"] --> f3["step"] --> f1
        f1 -- false --> f4["done"]
    end
```

One pass through the body is called an **iteration**.

## `while`

```cpp
int count{ 1 };
while (count <= 5)
{
    std::cout << count << ' ';
    ++count;
}
// 1 2 3 4 5
```

The condition is tested **before** each iteration. If it is false at the start, the body never runs. If nothing in the body ever makes it false, the loop never ends: an **infinite loop**.

## `do-while`

```cpp
int choice{};
do
{
    std::cout << "Enter 1 to 3: ";
    std::cin >> choice;
} while (choice < 1 || choice > 3);
```

The condition is tested **after** each iteration, so the body always runs at least once. That suits "ask, then check the answer". Note the `;` after the closing bracket.

## `for`

A counting loop needs three things: a starting value, a condition and a step. `for` puts all three on one line.

```cpp
//   start        condition   step
for (int i{ 0 };  i < 5;      ++i)
{
    std::cout << i << ' ';
}
// 0 1 2 3 4
```

Trace it:

| `i` | `i < 5`? | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | true | print 0, then `++i` |
| 1 | true | print 1, then `++i` |
| ... | | |
| 4 | true | print 4, then `++i` |
| 5 | false | the loop ends |

The patterns you will write most:

| To loop over | Write |
|---|---|
| 0 up to n − 1 (n iterations) | `for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i)` |
| 1 up to n | `for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i)` |
| 10 down to 1 | `for (int i{ 10 }; i > 0; --i)` |
| Every second value | `for (int i{ 0 }; i < 20; i += 2)` |

> [!tip] Start at 0, test with `<`
> Programmers count from zero because indexes start at zero. `for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i)` runs exactly `n` times and visits exactly the valid indexes of something with `n` elements. Make it your default shape.

## Which loop?

| Situation | Loop |
|---|---|
| You know how many iterations, or you are counting | `for` |
| You repeat until something happens, and it may already have happened | `while` |
| The body must run once before you can test | `do-while` |

## `break` and `continue`

```cpp
for (int i{ 1 }; i <= 10; ++i)
{
    if (i == 3)
    {
        continue;    // skip the rest of this iteration
    }
    if (i == 7)
    {
        break;       // leave the loop altogether
    }
    std::cout << i << ' ';
}
// 1 2 4 5 6
```

| Statement | Effect |
|---|---|
| `break` | Ends the loop immediately |
| `continue` | Ends this iteration; in a `for` loop the step still runs |

A loop written as `while (true)` relies on a `break` inside it to end. That is a normal pattern when the exit test belongs in the middle of the body.

## Nested loops

A loop inside a loop. The inner loop runs **in full** for every single iteration of the outer one.

```cpp
for (int row{ 1 }; row <= 3; ++row)
{
    for (int col{ 1 }; col <= 4; ++col)
    {
        std::cout << '*';
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}
```
```
****      outer loop: 3 iterations
****      inner loop: 4 iterations each time
****      12 stars in all
```

The inner loop's limit can depend on the outer variable. Changing `col <= 4` to `col <= row` gives a triangle:

```
*
**
***
```

## Building up a result

A very common shape: create a variable before the loop and update it on each iteration. That variable is called an **accumulator**.

```cpp
int sum{ 0 };
for (int i{ 1 }; i <= 100; ++i)
{
    sum += i;
}
std::cout << sum << '\n';    // 5050
```

The same shape counts things, finds a maximum, builds a string, and much more.

## Three classic bugs

| Bug | Cause | Check |
|---|---|---|
| **Off by one** | `<=` where you needed `<`, or the wrong start | Trace the first and the last iteration by hand |
| **Infinite loop** | Nothing in the body moves towards the exit | Ask what changes on each iteration |
| **Unsigned countdown** | `for (unsigned i{ 5 }; i >= 0; --i)` | An unsigned value is always `>= 0`, so the test never fails |

## Check yourself
```quiz
? How many times does `for (int i{ 0 }; i < 10; i += 3)` run?
- Three times
+ Four times
- Ten times
- Five times
> `i` takes the values 0, 3, 6 and 9. The next step makes it 12, which fails `i < 10`.

? When is `do-while` the right choice?
- When the loop may need to run zero times
- When you know exactly how many times to loop
+ When the body must run at least once, as in asking for input
- When the loop must count down instead of up
> `do-while` checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs once. That suits "ask, then check".

? What does `continue` do?
- It ends the loop completely
- It restarts the loop from the very first iteration
- It pauses the loop until the user presses a key
+ It skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next
> `continue` jumps to the next iteration; in a `for` loop the step still runs. `break` is the one that leaves the loop.

? An outer loop runs 5 times and its inner loop runs 6 times. How often does the inner body run?
- 11 times
+ 30 times
- 6 times
- 5 times
> The inner loop runs completely for each outer iteration: 5 × 6 = 30.
```
ideas:
1. Print every even number from 0 to 20.
2. Sum the digits of a whole number with a `while` loop, using `n % 10` and `n /= 10`.
3. Print a 10 by 10 multiplication table with nested loops and `std::setw(4)`.
